Index of continuous semi-Fredholm families, regularities
and semiregularities
M. Berkani
Abstract
In this paper, we deﬁne and index for continuous families of semi-Fredholm
bounded liner operators. Moreover, we study various regularities and semireg-
ularities of continuous families of bounded linear operators.

Introduction
In this part, we will introduce some deﬁnitions and notations that will be needed in
the next sections.
In [7], the concept of regularity was deﬁned by the following :
Definition 1.1. Let A be a unital Banach algebra, with unit e. A non-empty subset
R of A is called a regularity if it satisﬁes the following conditions:
i) If a ∈A and n ≥1, then a ∈R if and only if an ∈R.
ii) If a, b, c, d ∈L(X) are mutually commuting elements of A satisfying ac + bd = e,
then ab ∈R if and only if a, b ∈R .
A regularity R deﬁnes in a natural way a spectrum by σR(a) = {λ ∈C : a−λe /∈R},
for a ∈A. Moreover the spectrum σR satisﬁes the spectral mapping theorem.
Let X be an inﬁnite dimensional Banach space and L(X) be the Banach algebra
of bounded linear operators acting X. Various regularities of the Banach algebra
L(X) were studied in [7] and [1]. Here, we will consider similar regularities but for
continuous families of bounded linear operators.

Index of continuous semi-Fredholm families
In [2] and [3] respectively, we deﬁned an analytical index for continuous Fredholm
families of bounded linear operators into a Hilbert space (respectively into a Banach
space). Here, in the same way as in [2] and [3], we deﬁne an analytical index for
continuous semi-Fredholm families into a Banach space.
Let X be a topological space. Deﬁne an equivalence relation c on the space X by
setting that x c y, if and only if x and y belongs to the same connected component of
X. Let Xc be the quotient space associated to this equivalence relation. We extend
here the deﬁnition [3, Deﬁnition 1.1] of the index of a continuous family of Fredholm
operators to the case of a continuous family of semi-Fredholm operators.
Definition 2.1. The index of a continuous family of semi-Fredholm operators
T : X →L(X), parameterized by a topological space X is deﬁned by ind(T ) =
(ind(Tx))x∈Xc.
Thus the index of a continuous family of semi-Fredholm operators T is a sequence of
elements of Z = Z∪{−∞, +∞}, which may be a ﬁnite sequence or inﬁnite sequence,
depending on the cardinal nc of the connected components of X, which is assumed
here to have at most a countable set of connected components.
Theorem 2.2. The index of a continuous family of semi-Fredholm operators T
parameterized by a topological space X is well deﬁned as an element of Z nc. In
particular if X is reduced to a single element, then the index of T is equal to the
usual index of the semi-Fredholm operator T .
Proof. From the properties of the index [4, Chapter 4], it follows that two semi-
Fredholm operators located in the same connected component of the set of semi-
Fredholm operators have the same index. Moreover, as T is continuous, the image
of a connected component of the topological space X, is included in a connected
component of the set of semi-Fredholm operators. This shows that the index of a
family of semi-Fredholm operators is well deﬁned. Moreover, it is clear that if X is
reduced to a single element, the index of T deﬁned here is equal to the usual index
of the single semi-Fredholm operator T.
Definition 2.3. A continuous family K from X to L(X) is said to be compact if
Kx is compact for all x ∈X.
Proposition 2.4. i) Let T ∈C(X, SΦ(X)) be a continuous semi-Fredholm family
and let K be a continuous compact family. Then T + K is a semi-Fredholm family
and ind(T ) = ind(T + K).
ii) Let S, T ∈C(X, SΦ(X)) be two semi-Fredholm families, such that for all
x ∈X, Sx and Tx are both upper semi-Fredholm or both lower semi-Fredholm. Then
the family ST deﬁned by (ST )x = SxTx is a continuous semi-Fredholm family and
ind(ST ) = ind(S) + ind(T ).

Theorem 2.6. Let S, T be two semi-Fredholm homotopic elements of C(X, L(X)).
Then ind(T ) = ind(S).
Proof. Since S and T are semi-Fredholm homotopic, there exists a continuous map
h : X × [0, 1] →Fred(X) such that such that h(0, x) = S(x) and h(1, x) = T(x) for
all x ∈X. For a ﬁxed x ∈X, the map hx : [0, 1] →SΦ(X)), deﬁned by hx(t) = h(t, x)
is a continuous path in SΦ(X)) linking Sx to Tx. Since [0, 1] is connected and since
the usual index is constant on connected sets of SΦ(X), then ind(Sx) = ind(Tx).
Therefore ind(S) = ind(T ).

Upper and lower semiregularities of continuous fam-

Following [8], the axioms i) and ii) of regularities in Deﬁnition 1.1, are splitted in
two halves, each of them implying a one-way spectral mapping theorem and giving
raises to the notions of upper and lower semiregularities. We ﬁrst consider lower
semiregularities.
In all what follows, X will be a compact topological space. If R is an nonempty
subset of
C(X, L(X)), then for all x ∈X, we set Rx = {Tx | T ∈R}, x ∈X.
A- Upper semiregularities
Definition 4.1. Let A be a unital Banach algebra, with unit e. A non-empty subset
R of A is called a lower semiregularity if it satisﬁes the following conditions:
i) If a ∈A and an ∈R, n ≥1, then a ∈R.
ii) If a, b, c, d ∈A are mutually commuting elements of A satisfying ac + bd = e,
such that ab ∈R, then a, b ∈R .
If R is a lower semiregularity of A and a ∈A, we deﬁne the R-spectrum of a by
σR(a) = {λ ∈C/a −λe /∈R}.
Recall the following result from [8, Lemma 2]
Lemma 4.1. Let A be a unital Banach algebra with unit e and let R a lower
semiregularity of A. then:
1. e ∈R.
2. Inv(A) ⊂R, where Inv(A) is the set of invertible elements of A.
3. If a ∈R, b ∈Inv(A) and ab = ba, then ab ∈R.
4. σR(a) ⊂σ(a).

B- Upper semiregularities
We assume that R satisﬁes the following two conditions, summarized as condi-
tions (**) :
i) ∀x ∈X, ∀T ∈C(X, L(X)), Tx ∈Rx ⇒T ∈R.

Definition 4.4. Let A be a unital Banach algebra, with unit e. A non-empty subset
R of A is called an upper semiregularity if it satisﬁes the following conditions:
i) If a ∈A and a ∈R, then for all n ≥1, then an ∈R.
ii) If a, b, c, d ∈L(X) are mutually commuting elements of A satisfying ac + bd = e,
then if a, b ∈R, then ab ∈R .
iii) R contains a neighbourhood of the unit element e.
If R is a lower semiregularity of A and a ∈A, we deﬁne the R-spectrum of a by
σR(a) = {λ ∈C/a −λe /∈R}.
Using the properties of upper semiregularities, we obtain a one way spectral
mapping theorem. Here Inv(C(X, L(X)) and Inv(L(X)), denote respectively the
set of invertible elements of C(X, L(X) and L(X) .
Theorem 4.5. Let X be a compact topological space and let R be a nonempty subset
of C(X, L(X)), containing an open neighborhood of the identity I and satisfying the
conditions (**). Then:
1. R is an upper semiregularity of
C(X, L(X)).
2. Assume that:
∀x ∈X, if Tx ∈Rx ∩Inv(L(X)), then (Tx)−1 ∈R. (∗∗∗)
Then if f an analytic function in a neighborhood of the usual spectrum σ(T ) of
T which is non-constant on any connected component of σ(T ), then σR(f(T ) ⊂
